Abstract
This white paper presents the current design direction, subsystem architecture, and integration
plan for Howard University’s ASNE PEP:26 autonomous electric surface vessel. It contains key
decisions made across hull selection, digital geometry workflow, hydrostatic and CFD analysis,
propulsion architecture, electrical power system, control and autonomy stack, testing strategy,
and final integration path.
The selected deep-V hull remains the physical backbone of the project because it provides a
balance of payload capability, internal volume, stability, and hydrodynamic performance. The
design process combines multiple modeling and analysis tools to ensure accurate geometry,
reliable mass properties, and drag evaluation.
At this stage, work is centered on electrical setup, control system, and internal subsystem
integration. These efforts are intended to streamline full system installation with the hull,
allowing for efficient mounting, wiring, and validation. Following integration, the vessel will
undergo staged testing, beginning in controlled pool conditions and progressing to open-water
operation.
1. Introduction
The ASNE PEP:26 autonomy competition requires student teams to design, build, and
demonstrate an electrically powered surface vessel that can operate safely and under real mission
constraints. It requires a system that can carry the required payload, survive launch and
operation, manage electrical power responsibly, be controlled, remain stable in the water, and
maintain enough hydrodynamic efficiency to complete the mission without exhausting the
available onboard energy. For Howard University’s team, that means the project must be treated
as a full system-integration problem in which hull choice, propulsion method, battery strategy,
control architecture, and test planning all influence one another.
The work completed to date establishes the analytical and physical foundation needed for that
system-level approach. The team defined project requirements, reviewed prior PEP outcomes,
and investigated practical limits imposed by competition rules such as voltage, expectations,
safety requirements, and launch-readiness constraints. From there, the project moved into hull
selection, CAD development, hydrostatic calculations, CFD setup, electrical architecture
planning, and early decisions regarding actuation, control, cooling, and onboard packaging.
Those tasks were not independent. Hull draft affects drag modeling; drag affects thrust
requirements; thrust requirements affect voltage and battery decisions; those power choices
affect thermal management, wiring size, and the control electronics that must command the
hardware.
This white paper organizes that work into a technical narrative. It emphasizes the material that
explains what the vessel is, why the team chose this direction, what subsystems will be

2. System Overview – PEP26 Autonomous Vessel
2.1 Hull Selection Approach
Hull selection was treated as a primary systems decision because it directly affects payload
capability, stability, drag behavior, packaging volume, and downstream integration. Rather than
selecting a hull only on appearance or availability, the team used a weighted design matrix to
compare candidate hulls against the requirements most important to PEP:26. The scoring
framework assigned the highest weight to payload requirements, followed by hydrodynamic
efficiency, assembly practicality, cost, and transportability. Using this approach, the selected
configuration, labeled Hull 5 in the study, achieved the strongest weighted score at 3.15 and was
therefore chosen as the basis for continued design work.

The final choice is a deep-V hull. This geometry was favored because it offers a more balanced
response to the actual operating conditions expected in competition. Compared with flatter or
less volume-efficient alternatives, the deep-V hull provides better confidence in carrying the
required payload while still maintaining hydrodynamic performance and an internal envelope for
electronics, power hardware, and mounting structures.

pages.text:
The current PEP:26 vessel is based on a 76-inch deep-V fiberglass monohull (Scarab hull),
selected through a weighted study that evaluated payload capacity, internal volume,
hydrodynamic performance, assembly practicality, and transportability.
This hull was chosen primarily because it provides the internal space needed to integrate the
battery, propulsion hardware, control electronics, and supporting structure without creating
packaging or stability issues. Several alternative hulls either limited internal layout flexibility or
introduced concerns with balance and usable volume.
The deep-V geometry also supports more predictable behavior in the water, which is important
for both manual operation and the development of autonomous control. A commercially
manufactured hull was used to reduce structural uncertainty and allow the team to focus on
system integration and performance-critical subsystems. This decision keeps the project aligned
with the timeline while maintaining a reliable physical platform for testing and validation.

2.2 Propulsion System (Thruster-Based)
The propulsion system was redirected from a traditional propeller-shaft configuration to a
thruster-based setup due to procurement constraints. This shift allowed the team to move forward
with a configuration that could be reliably sourced, integrated, and tested into the system.
The current setup uses two 24V Blue Robotics thrusters at the rear as the primary propulsion
units, and two 12V Blue Robotics thruster at the front for directional control and turning
assistance.
This configuration allows the rear thrusters to provide forward propulsion while enabling
steering through differential thrust. The front thruster supports turning, particularly at low
speeds, where precise maneuvering is required.

Each thruster is driven by a dedicated Blue Robotics Basic ESC (Electronic Speed Controller),
which regulates power delivery and allows for smooth, controlled actuation based on input
signals.

24V Thruster
2.3 Control System Architecture
The control system is structured to support manual operation, allowing the boat to be tested
safely.A radio transmitter and receiver system is used for manual control. The receiver acts as the
interface between user input and the onboard system, sending throttle and directional signals to
the ESCs.
The ESCs receive these signals and regulate power delivery to each thruster. Proper ESC
calibration ensures that both rear thrusters respond consistently, which is important for stable
differential steering.

pages.text:
The initial hull geometry was developed in Fusion 360 based on the selected 76-inch Scarab
deep-V hull. Both outer and inner hull profiles were modeled to define the physical structure and
internal layout of components. These early models provided the foundation for further
refinement and simulation.

3.2 Geometry Refinement (Rhino3D)
The geometry was refined in Rhino3D to improve surface continuity and ensure a clean,
watertight model suitable for simulation. This step was necessary to eliminate gaps and
inconsistencies that caused early CFD failures.

3.3 DelftShip Modeling and Hydrostatic Analysis
DelftShip Pro was used to generate a more accurate hull representation and evaluate hydrostatic
behavior, including draft, displacement, and buoyancy distribution.

pages.text:
Earlier estimates using a block coefficient predicted a draft of about 3.7 inches, but this
underestimated the true submerged volume. Using DelftShip’s hydrostatic calculations, the
correct displacement (~0.070 m³) corresponded to a draft of approximately 7.5 inches, which
better reflects the actual vessel weight and geometry.
This corrected draft was critical for ensuring realistic CFD setup and proper hull positioning
relative to the free surface.

3.4 CFD Setup and Boundary Conditions
CFD simulations were conducted in ANSYS Fluent to determine hydrodynamic drag and
validate the design. The hull geometry was imported from DelftShip as a clean IGES model and
placed at the correct draft.
A multiphase VOF (air + water) model was used to capture free-surface effects such as wave
formation and wake behavior. Gravity was included to allow the waterline to form naturally.
The simulation domain was defined relative to hull length to avoid boundary interference. Final
domain sizing was selected after independence testing and set to:
Upstream: 5L ; Downstream: 12L; Sides: 5L; Bottom: 4L; Top: 3L
Mesh refinement was applied around the hull using a poly-hex core mesh. A fine mesh level was
selected after mesh independence testing, balancing accuracy and computational cost.
Boundary conditions included a velocity inlet (7 m/s), pressure outlet, symmetry side walls, a noslip hull surface, and a sufficiently deep bottom boundary to prevent artificial confinement
effects.

The free-surface results showed realistic bow and stern wave formation, confirming that the

selection.

pages.text:
3.6 Final Result
Correcting the draft from 3.7 inches to ~7.5 inches and transitioning to a multiphase CFD model
were the two most important steps in obtaining reliable hydrodynamic results.

The VOF free-surface visualization confirms that the simulation is producing physically realistic
behavior at 7 m/s. The bow wave forms correctly at the leading edge, the wake pattern is stable
and coherent, and the water–air interface does not show numerical breakup. This indicates that
the multiphase model, mesh, and boundary conditions are performing as intended.
4. System Integration
4.1 Mechanical Integration
Mechanical integration focuses on securely mounting all major components within the hull while
maintaining proper weight distribution and accessibility. The battery, thrusters, and electronics
are positioned to keep the center of gravity low and centered, improving stability. Mounting
brackets and supports are used to prevent movement during operation and testing.
4.2 Electrical Integration
Electrical integration involves connecting the battery, ESCs, thrusters, and control system in a
clean and organized layout. Power wiring is routed to minimize losses and avoid interference
with signal lines. All connections are secured to ensure reliability during operation, especially
under varying loads from the propulsion system.

pages.text:
4.3 Waterproofing and Structural Considerations
Waterproofing is implemented to protect internal electronics from water exposure during testing
and operation. Key components are enclosed, and cable entry points are sealed to prevent leaks.
Structural considerations focus on ensuring the hull can support system weight and withstand
water forces without compromising performance.

System Integration

5. Testing and Validation Plan
5.1 Component-Level Testing:
Testing has been completed for the thrusters to ensure power and movement of the
haul. The 24 V battery was connected to the ESC which is connected to the receiver
and thruster. The thruster was then but in a bucket of water to simulate the boat and
successfully ran trails.
5.2 Pool Testing
Pool testing shall be conducted April 1 in the Howard University Gymnasium Pool
6. Risk Considerations
1. Size: By using a narrow haul, there are potential risks of controlling and managing the
boat turning operations.
2. Weight/Center of Gravity: Due to the smaller nature of the selected haul, risks could arise
within the heaviness of our two batteries. In addition, the added weights needed to
successfully compete could also weigh the haul down more than anticipated. Once fully
mounted, the location and positioning of the weight is critical to the hauls' ability to
withstand waves and stay afloat during the competition.

3. Temperature: As a result of having nearly 50 volts to power our boat, the heat released by
our system will be significant over the span of a race. However, to accommodate this, we
aim to address this with efficient cooling.
7. Next Steps
The next steps in developing our boat are to integrate our electrical systems into our hull.
Additionally, upon integrating we will look to test our boat in realistic conditions to better
understand performance and to refine our design.
